comments.text: How can they take their house with out compensation or authorization?  That would be grand theft.  google: Grand theft is a criminal offense involving the unlawful taking of another person's property with the intent to permanently deprive the owner of it. It is distinguished from petty theft by the high value of the stolen goods or by the specific type of property taken.  o secure a grand theft conviction, prosecutors generally must prove three primary elements:Unlawful Taking: Physically moving, using, or appropriating property without the owner's authorization.Specific Intent: A conscious objective to permanently (or in some cases temporarily) deprive the owner of their property or its benefits.Value Threshold: The market value of the stolen goods meets or exceeds a state-mandated limit (typically ranging from \(\$750\) to \(\$1,200\), depending on the state). When Does Theft Become "Grand"?While definitions and thresholds vary heavily by jurisdiction (e.g., Cornell Law School's Grand Theft Guide details specific state variances), the crime is usually escalated to grand theft in two main ways:Monetary Value: Stealing money, goods, or property whose cumulative fair market value exceeds the state's statutory limit.Property Type: Stealing certain high-risk or protected items automatically triggers a grand theft charge, regardless of their actual cash value. Common examples include firearms, automobiles, farm animals, and emergency medical equipment. Legal ConsequencesBecause grand theft is a more severe form of theft than petty larceny, it is almost always prosecuted as a felony. Depending on the specific state and the total value of the stolen property, penalties can range from mandatory restitution and probation to several years or decades in state prison
